newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr bruised but unbowed after savage fall.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr bruised but unbowed after savage fall.

text.p: The Australian dollar on Wednesday struggled to hold 79.5 U.S. cents after its biggest fall in a decade when markets overnight reacted to talk of lower rates, stripping it of almost three cents from a peak of 81 U.S. cents.
The fall, however, was seen as an opportunity by local exporters and investment funds desperate to take foreign exchange cover.
"It was a dream come true to these guys and they bought in serious size," said Michael Workman, a currency analyst at the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA).
"That makes me think the dollar's heading higher after all."
But by 4.30 pm (0530 GMT) the currency was struggling to hold US$0.7975/80 having bounced from a deep offshore low of US$0.7855, but was still far below Tuesday's late US$0.8135/40.

On the crosses, it steadied at 90.25/35 yen after plunging as far as 88.78 overnight, but again was a long way short of Tuesday's late 92.95/05. In trade weighted terms it was sharply lower at 59.1 from a previous 60.5 finish.
This was a savage turn in fortunes for the currency which only Monday had been celebrating a six-year high of US$0.8212 and a four-year peak on the yen at 93.80.
The ostensible cause of the setback was Bernie Fraser.
Fraser is a former governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) and his word carried great weight with the market until he retired in September.

So when he told a current affairs television programme here on Tuesday night that there was room for lower rates in Australia, some offshore investors reacted as though he was still in charge of the central bank.
"Certainly if you look at what happened, it seems to have followed on from his comments," said Steve Shuster, head of foreign exchange operations at Citibank Australia.
"But there's more to it than that," Shuster added.
Pressures had been brewing since the dollar launched itself from US$0.7815 a month ago, reaching US$0.8212 in a frenzy of offshore buying last week.
The entire five percent rise came without a meaningful correction leaving the market, and short-term momentum investors in particular, dangerously long.
"What you had was a big snowball reaction," said Shuster. "The move above 82 cents, and then back down below 81, and 80 after that, triggered sell levels for a lot of long positions."

"It's difficult to say it was very overdone because the market was obviously very long and what we'll find now is it will struggle to trade back through 82 U.S. cents," he said. That was much the same verdict of chart analysts who were deflated by the rupture of so many support levels.
"I hate to say it, but this looks like being the mid-point of a year-long consolidation period," said Darren Spain, a currency analyst with Credit Suisse in New York.
"We've had seven months since the former peak in May, and it could be a few more until the uptrend resumes once more."
He looked for a base to form at US$0.7850 with a ceiling around US$0.8070 or, at most, US$0.8150.

The fundamental support of relatively high yields had not changed, however, with the RBA staying silent this morning despite all the talk an easing would follow the monthly meeting of its policy board on Tuesday.
Analysts interpreted this as a sign rates would remain steady at 6.5 percent until January at the earliest, thus keeping the dollar's yield premium intact for another month.
"At the end of the day, the Aussie will grind higher because the Japanese will keep buying it," said Workman at CBA.
"Rates look set to stay at record lows so yields here will be attractive whether the RBA moves or not," he said.
